tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReadNotifications

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write

# Running The Room — course export

The export covers all **31 lesson entries** in the course inventory: 28 lessons across Modules 1–4 and 3 Free Sample entries. Each entry has a downloaded media file, a timestamped transcript, and a transcript-based summary. Files are organized in the Drive folder's existing module and lesson folders.

See **Old Bull course inventory.csv** for each lesson's title, course post, Wistia ID, relative media/transcript/summary paths, and whether the Drive transcript and summary matched the local copies by SHA-256. The final audit found **31/31 complete**.

Transcripts were generated locally with faster-whisper `small.en`. They are **unverified machine drafts**; names, technical terms, and punctuation may be wrong. Summaries are based on those drafts and include approximate media timestamps. Check important passages against the original audio before sharing or relying on them for clinical or operational decisions. Examples and claims in the videos are the speaker's account, not independently validated here.

To download another Wistia video in PowerShell, use its ID from the player or the inventory:

```powershell
& "$env:USERPROFILE\bin\yt-dlp.exe" -f "best[ext=mp4]" -o "Lesson title.%(ext)s" "wistia:VIDEO_ID"
```

For an audio lesson, use `-f best`. A newly opened terminal may also recognize `yt-dlp` directly if your updated PATH has loaded.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\new-project

# New project scaffold

Every project Eric works on lives in one folder under DEV, is its own git repo, and has a private remote at `github.com/erash11/<name>`. This skill creates that shape in one pass so every project starts identical on either machine.

## DEV root

- Mac: `~/DEV`
- Windows: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`
- Football sub-projects live in `DEV/Football/<name>` and are still their own repos.
- `DEV/_DRIVE` is a link to the Google Drive primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables). Never create a project inside it and never `git init` it.

If the cwd is already the intended project folder, use it. Otherwise ask for the project name only; everything else is fixed.

## Steps

1. Create `DEV/<name>` (or use the existing folder). Do not nest a repo inside another repo; check `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` from the parent first.
2. `git init -b main` if there is no `.git`.
3. Write these files if they do not exist. Never overwrite an existing one; append the Session routine section to an existing AGENTS.md if it is missing.

`AGENTS.md`:
```
# AGENTS.md

Project: <name>

## What this is
<one paragraph, ask Eric if unknown>

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.
```

`CLAUDE.md`: exactly one line, `@AGENTS.md`.

`docs/STATUS.md`:
```
# STATUS

Read this first. Update it before ending every session.

## Current state
- <today>: project created.

## Next
-

## Open questions
-

## Gotchas
-
```

`.gitignore`: `.env`, `.env.*`, `node_modules/`, `.venv/`, `venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, plus any data folder Eric names.

4. `git add -A && git commit -m "Scaffold project"`.
5. `gh repo create erash11/<name> --private --source=. --push`. If the repo already exists, add it as origin and `git push -u origin main` instead.
6. Confirm in two lines: folder path and repo URL. Remind Eric that the other machine gets it with `gh repo clone erash11/<name>` into its DEV.

## Rules

- Repo name = folder name; replace spaces with underscores.
- Never create a repo for anything holding identifiable health or athlete medical data (DexaProject is the precedent). Ask if unsure.
- Do not add a `docs/context.md` unless there is cloud-project context to transfer.

Private repo. Docs only; no media/PDFs committed.

input.prompt:
Build a context brief on Eric Rash's current job situation so another agent can write staff-development and department-building recommendations for him. Eric is Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. He is an OKR-driven change agent in a status-quo group, "authors direction when leadership does not", supervisor reports go biweekly to Kenny Boyd and Chris Ruf, and his career target is an analytics-first player-coach role near Iowa around mid-2027 (so anything he builds should survive his departure). Staff-facing terms: Athletic Performance (not S&C), Athletic Medicine (not sports medicine), Applied Performance (not sport science).

DEV root (Git Bash): `/c/Users/eric_rash/Desktop/DEV`. Read-only; do not modify any repo. Read what exists of these (skip what is missing; use docs/STATUS.md and README-level docs first, do not read code or raw data):
- `ContextVault/Career-Context-Document.md`, `ContextVault/personal_constitution.md`, `ContextVault/docs/`
- `OKRs_2026-27/docs/`
- `Department_Audits/README.md`, `Department_Audits/docs/` (the .docx audit plans: extract text with python-docx if available, e.g. `python -c`, or skip if not possible)
- `Intern_Curriculum/`, `Supervisor_Reviews/`, `Education_Alignment_Initiative/`, `Performance_Playbook/`, `SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/`, `Tech_Inventory_Analysis/`, `Sport_Tech_Vetting/`, `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc/`, `BAIR_Steering_Committee/`, `Transformative_Athlete_Experience/`, `Program_Context_Meet/`, `CPSS_BaylorSportScience_Curriculum/`, `Weekly_Research_Review/`, `KeystoneOS/docs/STATUS.md` (docs/STATUS.md, README, AGENTS.md, and key docs only)
- Workspace maps: `CLAUDE.md`, `PERFORMANCE.md`, `PROGRAM.md` at DEV root
- Memory: `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\global-memory\MEMORY.md`, `USER.md`; and search `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\projects\*\memory\` for files named like `*prioritization-slate*`, `*okr*`, `*supervisor*`, `*staff*`, `*tech-inventory*`. Also try `memsearch search "<q>" --top-k 5` for: "staff development", "prioritization slate", "OKR gate AI integration data governance", "Kitman MyLink", "staff meeting", "department structure staff roles".

Do NOT include athlete names or any athlete health/medical information in your output. Staff names and roles are fine.

Write `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\RunningTheRoom\notes\eric-context.md` with sections:
1. `## Role and remit`: Eric's job, who he reports to, what he owns.
2. `## Staff and structure`: who is on the Applied Performance staff and adjacent groups (Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, interns, GAs), roles, known strengths/gaps, reporting lines, as far as the sources say.
3. `## Active projects and initiatives`: each with one line of status and its source path (OKRs, prioritization slate, department audit, tech inventory, intern curriculum, education initiatives, research review series, RTP work, Kitman vs MyLink, etc.).
4. `## Existing forums and vehicles`: recurring meetings, reports, curricula, and documents Eric already runs or controls (biweekly status report, staff meetings, OKR meeting prep, research-in-5, newsletters, etc.).
5. `## Pending decisions and blockers`.
6. `## Constraints`: IT/cloud limits, culture (status quo group), time horizon (mid-2027 exit target), season timing (it is 2026-09-24, mid football season), anything else.
7. `## Career and values frame`: short, only what bears on how he leads staff.
8. `## Sources read`: list of paths.

Plain direct prose, no em dashes. Mark anything inferred as "(inferred)". Return a 5-line summary when done.

The context brief flags a late-July all-staff care-team restructure as unread detail: find it via the source paths listed in eric-context.md (read-only) and fold in what bears on staff structure. Do not modify any other repo.

What Eric asked for, verbatim intent: (1) a short summary of what this material is; (2) a detailed plan for using this material to construct a high-performance department; (3) from that plan plus his current context, job situation, and everything going on, recommendations on how to proceed with developing his staff and continuing certain projects.

Write:

1. `docs/00_what_this_is.md`: SHORT (300-500 words). What the course is, who made it, the four modules and their through-line in one line each, the handful of tools worth keeping, and a caveat that transcripts are unverified whisper drafts and PDFs are authoritative.

2. `docs/01_department_plan.md`: the detailed plan to build a high-performance department from this material. Generic enough to be a real operating model, but written for a university athletics setting (Applied Performance, Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine). Structure it as phases (foundation: common language and people; technology and measurement discipline; meeting and communication operating rhythm; integration and decision pathways), each with: objective, which course tools are used (named, with note/PDF references), concrete steps, artifacts produced, who owns it, and how you know it worked (observable adoption signals, not documents produced). Include a section on what must be installed so it survives the leader leaving (the "operating system" vs what the leader personally carries). Include a sequencing rationale and a dependency map (a simple table is fine).

3. `docs/02_recommendations.md`: the specific recommendations for Eric. Hard requirements:

# What this material is

"Running The Room" is a paid online course from Old Bull Performance, written and presented by Dr Jason Weber (former AFL high-performance manager, creator of the SpeedSig gait product). It is for people who lead or want to lead a high-performance department. The material is 31 lessons (webinars, short video labs, three podcasts) and 26 PDFs (blogs, cheat sheets, worksheets, workbooks) across four modules. The course files label the fourth block "Module 6"; the Drive folder and these notes call it Module 4.

The argument in one sentence: departments buy technology faster than they build the people, language and procedures needed to turn it into decisions, and the fix is discipline written down.

## The four modules

- **Module 1, People, language and discipline before technology.** Audit staff on a knowledge and behaviour grid, agree a common language (means before modality before technology), and inventory the tech stack by what it measures, not by brand.
- **Module 2, Turning technology into defensible decisions.** Separate measurement from inference, map every tool to a question and an owner, decide whether a metric is monitored or tested, pre-agree decision gates, and quantify noise so the gates hold.
- **Module 3, Discipline equals freedom.** Meeting problems are meeting-type problems: name the modality (Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build), time-box, pre-read, log every decision with an owner and review date, and use meetings as leadership reps for staff.
- **Module 4, The integration problem.** Sound technical work fails at five breakpoints (language, pathway, authority, relationship, process); structure the clinical to training grey zone with ownership, empowerment and communication rules; build dissent into the decision log.

## Tools worth keeping

| Tool | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix and Student Workbook | module-1 note; Lab_1b_Blog pp.1-3; Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook pp.1-5 |
| Means, modality, technology ordering and the CM² athlete map | module-1 note; Lab_1A_Blog pp.1-3 |
| Tech Stack Reality Check (inventory, reliability, one-page procedure) | module-1 note; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit pp.1-4 |
| Measured, inferred, probability, next step communication | module-2 note; Lab_2a pp.3-4 |
| Capability and Workflow Matrix | module-2 note; Lab_2b pp.2-3 |
| Monitoring vs testing rule and the five coach questions | module-2 note; Lab_2c pp.1-2 |
| Five-part decision gate and the MDC95 / SWC decision logic | module-2 note; Lab_2D pp.1-2; Lab_2E pp.1-2 |
| Meeting typology cheat sheet, Kaigi, Stoplight slide, decision log, Lab 3D rep worksheet | module-3 note; Lab_3b cheat sheet pp.1-2; Lab_3a pp.1-3; Lab_3c template pp.1-2; Lab_3D_Worksheet pp.1-3 |
| Grey Zone Workbook (people profile, operational logic, phase ownership, empowerment, communication) | module-4 note; The_Grey_Zone_Workbook pp.2-11 |
| Six-check evidence stack and Bias Prompt Analysis | module-2 note; Stacking_Evidence pp.2-4; module-4 note; Structured_Thinking pp.6-7 |

## Caveat on sources

The lesson transcripts are unverified faster-whisper drafts with frequent mis-hearings. The PDFs are the authoritative source and are cited by page wherever a claim rests on them. Anything marked transcript-only in the module notes (the six-stage decision pathway, the Webinar 3 operating practices, the go/no-go run order, the 20-minute meeting rules) is the speaker's spoken account with no written backup. Course media and PDFs stay on Drive and are never committed here.

The handover test is the six-stage pathway's expertise-gap question: is there a high-clarity handover when staff change, with thresholds, their origin and their reviewer written down?

Count adoption signals (a second person uses it, a coach declines to react to noise, a meeting ends with a logged decision).

The July reset (advance notice, email now, website later) fixed the launch loop but not the medium: decks nobody asked for, pushed to a mixed audience. The course's cheaper route is Lab 3D: education happens inside meetings you already run, one topic, one slide, one time box, then a debrief (Lab_3D_Blog pp.1-2). This is where Lab 3D reps happen. | Cheat sheet pp.1-2; Lab_3a p.2; Lab_3D worksheet | outlives, portfolio |

docs/02_recommendations.md:99:Evidence: "training wheels on"; you teach procedures and data-management practice; summer onboarding KR scored 0.0. That score is evidence about your onboarding, not about Noah, and should be read that way. Basketball is self-contained and resistant, so adoption is not a fair measure of him. Position after the GA term is an open question to Chris.
docs/02_recommendations.md:130:Run the Student Workbook before you place anyone else. Your own answer to Option A or Option B (do you teach the framework, or empower the person who can) decides whether the education KR is yours at all (Module_6B_Part_B p.2). The brief says you know you under-educated colleagues on what the unit does; the course says constant re-explanation is diagnostic evidence, and the fix is education early, in the forums, not translation on demand.

### Linda

Evidence: role under Applied Performance still being defined; leadership stated your role is supportive, not directive; two August meetings produced four candidate projects for Tennis and Athletic Performance. No knowledge or behaviour evidence in any source.

Placement: none. Do not place her on the matrix on this evidence. Use the Lab 1B probes gently instead: ask what she is working on for CPD; invite one ten-minute presentation at the staff meeting on the project she cares most about.

Delegate: the means question. Of the four projects, which one has a receiver, a question, and a monitor-or-test answer (Lab_2c p.2)? Pick that one with her and drop the other three from the list until it ships. Four projects with no owner and no receiver is the pattern that ended your own earlier planning systems.

Watch for: the permission gate. Her role sits with Chris; anything directive is claimed ground. Tag: now.

### Student workers

Unnamed, uncounted in the sources. Give them the Lab 1C step 1 inventory (measurement-system tables for the devices they touch) and one procedure to follow exactly; procedure adherence is the check. Tag: outlives.

### You

Run the Student Workbook before you place anyone else. Your own answer to Option A or Option B (do you teach the framework, or empower the person who can) decides whether the education KR is yours at all (Module_6B_Part_B p.2). The brief says you know you under-educated colleagues on what the unit does; the course says constant re-explanation is diagnostic evidence, and the fix is education early, in the forums, not translation on demand.

## 6. Project-by-project calls

| Project | Call | Why | Course principle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tech_Inventory_Analysis (KR 1.1, due 10-09) | Continue | Has a receiver, a date, closed data. Plan-agreed step is overdue; send it as a two-option email this week. | Kaigi prerequisites (Lab_3a p.1) |
| HPI_Protocol v1 (KR 1.2) | Reshape | One filled matrix column for one sport (owners, workflow, monitor or test label) instead of a platform. Whether HPI is a Baylor framework or an implementation is still open with Kenny; the column answers it. | Means first; Lab_2b matrix; Lab_2c rule |
| Education_Curriculum (KR 2.1, four pieces) | Reshape | Two pieces by Oct 15; continue to four only on a documented adoption signal. Redirect saved hours to the reliability table. | Lab 3D: education in meetings; adoption over documents |
| RTP_Constraints_Course (KR 2.2) | Continue | Real receiver, one real session is a real adoption test. Add the four-part report form and one gate exercise. | Lab_2a pp.3-4; Lab_2D |
| WomensHealth_Survey (KR 3.1) | Continue | Pure handover with a data dictionary; low course relevance; finish it. | Procedures as IP (Lab_1c p.3) |
| NCAA_BestPractices_Doc (Spring) | Reshape | Make the continuity plan the matrix, the procedures and the empowerment checklist, not prose. The doc is the wrapper. | Operating system vs leader (plan, "What must survive the leader leaving") |
| RTP Working Group (Health & Wellness) | Hold; offer through Chris | The gaps overview already went to Kenny and named the staff-education gaps (new-hire manual, presentation series, movement-skill workshops). Those are the one-page procedures and Lab 3D reps prescribed here. Under the new Athlete Health structure it is claimed ground; offer the artifacts, do not run the group. | Lab_1c p.3; Lab_3D worksheet; Grey Zone ownership map |
| Sport-facing data pipelines (ForceDecks workbook, GPS load reporting, Kinexon volleyball, CMJ dashboard, S2, CATES, injury surveillance) | Continue | These are the workflows the pillars sit on and several are single-person builds. Each needs a named QC owner and a procedure page; the day-30 ForceDecks procedure is the first instance. Run the dirty-data and expertise-gap questions on each before the next staff change. | Lab 6D audit (transcript-only); Lab_1c p.3 |
| SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework | Pause (already parked) | Approval now sits with general counsel and ITS per July 29. Keep the three-question routing sheet; add "what question does it answer" as question zero. | Means, modality, technology |
| Research in 5 | Continue, reshape format | Readout = stoplight. Lead with the recommendation. Count replies and uses. | Lab_3c; 20-second rule |
| Education_Alignment_Initiative | Pause | Over-scoped against Lab 3D. Harvest the deck design system. | One topic, one slide, one time box |
| Intern_Curriculum / CPSS | Reshape | Module 1 = Lab 1C submission. No further modules without a cohort. | Lab_1c p.4 |
| Performance_Playbook | Continue | It is the home for the operating system. | Procedures manual (Webinar 3, transcript-only) |
| Department_Audits | Pause | An unsponsored audit hits the permission gate. The course's cheaper audits (K-B, 1C, matrix gap list) replace it this year. | Know thyself first (Lab_1b) |
| BAIR Steering Committee | Hold at email oversight | When a proposal needs a call, run it as a Kaigi by email: options, date, log. Do not schedule the first meeting in-season. | Kaigi by pre-read |
| Program_Context_Meet | Reshape | Run two (Volleyball and one other), 20 minutes each, with the five coach questions folded in. | Lab_2c coach script |
| Briefing Asset | Reshape | Becomes the annual unit report Doug asked for. Submit through Chris. Drop the SPA meeting ask. | Leadership asset (Lab_2b p.3) |
| Sport_Tech_Vetting | Stop as standalone | Folded already. The decision matrix collapses to one question: means, then modality, then technology. | Lab_1A ordering |
| AI integration initiative | Park | Policy-restricted; pilot done. Log the park with a review date. | Decision log |
| Athlete data governance | Hold to Oct 15, then park | Waiting on an external proposal since May. If it arrives, one section in the NCAA doc. | Gate with a timeframe (Lab_2D p.2) |
| Kitman vs MyLink | Decide by Oct 15 | Two options, information exists, one spender. Also ask the means question: which cell of the matrix does the platform fill that the current stack cannot? If none, the answer may be neither. | Kaigi; means first |
| White paper | Keep parked | Blake credited; no receiver pressure this semester. | Slate cap |
| Research repository MVP | Stop | Near zero twice; no receiver. | If not in a workflow it does not exist |
| Transformative_Athlete_Experience | Stop | No receiver, no date. | Same |
| Newsletter | Already stopped | Replaced by the education KR; do not revive. | Same |

## 7. Honest constraints

- **In-season.** AJ owns football operations. Nothing in the 30/60/90 touches football operations, football staff communications or the load model. The empowerment checklist is written about what already happens; it changes nothing on the field until Spring.
- **No budget, no protected time.** Every step below is under two hours except the Lab 2E reliability work, which is why that one has an honest "unknown with an off-season plan" fallback.
- **Baylor IT.** The decision log goes in Teams because Teams is the institutional surface that survives you. Not DEV, not the vault, not Drive.
- **Status-quo culture.** "If you're unhappy, go figure it out" is the environment. The course's response is procedures as the transparent way to find out who can work inside a collaborative system (Module_6B_Part_A p.2). You can only apply that inside your own unit.
- **Education 0-for-3, twice.** Named in section 2. The medium is the problem, not the launch.
- **Mid-2027 exit.** Items tagged "outlives" are worth doing only if AJ or a successor is named to carry them. If Chris will not have that conversation by December, downgrade every "outlives" item to "portfolio" and do only the cheap version.
- **Permission gate.** Section 1's rule. The care-team and advisory-group offers go through Chris in writing, once, and then wait.
- **Portfolio value, stated plainly.** The decision log, the matrix with a reliability column, the rep ladder with a debriefed junior, and the empowerment checklist are the four artifacts that show department-building rather than analysis. Each is also the right thing to do here. That is the whole reason to prefer them over another deck.

## 8. 30/60/90

Anchored to Oct 15 (checkpoint) and Dec 18 (semester close). Nothing here breaks in-season work.

### First week (by Oct 1). Three actions, under two hours total.

1. **K-B self-audit into your PD folder** (45 minutes). Workbook B1 to B3 and D1. It is due Sept 30 anyway. Tag: now.
2. **Rewrite two invites** (20 minutes). The next Applied Performance staff meeting and the next AJ 1:1: modality, objective, duration, required prep, on the invite itself. Create the Teams channel for the decision log and paste the CSV header from the stoplight template (Lab_3c template p.2). Tag: outlives.
3. **Send Kenny the overdue plan-agreed email for the tech inventory** (20 minutes). Two options for the deliverable shape, a date, one question. That is a Kaigi by email. Tag: now.

Also owed, not new work: status report #3, with the Decisions Needed lines in stoplight form.

### By day 30 (Oct 24)

- First staff meeting run with named segments and a log entry. AJ on audit. Noah rep 1 (ops stand-up segment).
- Kitman vs MyLink decided with Chris by Oct 15 and logged.
- Oct 15 checkpoint run as an AAR: education KR cut to two unless an adoption signal exists; OKR gate logged (AI parked, governance held or parked).
- Tech inventory shipped 10-09 with the workflow filter applied to the retention question.
- Lab 1C submission for one device you run yourself (ForceDecks CMJ is the obvious one): inventory line, raw signal, derived metric, reliability source, one-page procedure into the Performance_Playbook SOP template. One page. Tag: outlives, portfolio.
- Program_Context_Meet run once (Volleyball), with the five coach questions.

### By day 60 (Nov 23)

- Capability and Workflow Matrix, one column for one sport, ten cells, owners named. This is HPI v1's scope; say so in the status report.
- Reliability table for the top five metrics, or "unknown" with a written off-season repeat-testing plan per row.
- AJ's first ten-minute presentation. Football empowerment checklist drafted with him in a 1:1, de facto rows marked.
- Noah rep 2 (stoplight slide with error band stated).
- Research in 5 issued in readout format; count replies.
- ITS stand-up running if Micah answers the re-sent request; three-bullet report-out to Cody, Jovon and Kenny after each.
- Annual unit report drafted from the briefing asset, submitted through Chris.

### By day 90 (Dec 18)

- Semester close AAR: count decisions logged, actions closed on time, reps completed. Those three numbers go in the last status report of the semester.
- AJ's lanes for Spring written and agreed with Chris. The succession conversation had, whatever its answer.
- Noah reps 3 and 4 done; his procedure page in the playbook.
- One page to Chris offering, for Spring: the typology cheat sheet for one sport administrator's care team, and one Grey Zone walkthrough with Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance for one sport. Offered once, in writing.
- NCAA best-practices scope set as matrix plus procedures plus checklist.
- Intern module 1 rewritten as the Lab 1C submission.

## 9. Open questions only you can answer

1. Is AJ the successor, and will you say so to him and to Chris before December? Every "outlives" item depends on the answer.
2. Which ground is yours in the new structure: does Chris want you in the advisory-group and care-team conversations, or is Carrie the door and Chris the messenger?
3. Will you actually cut the education KR to two pieces on Oct 15 if there is no adoption signal, on the third cycle, knowing it will look like retreat?
4. Kitman vs MyLink: what question does either platform answer that the current stack cannot? If you cannot name the matrix cell, is the honest answer neither?
5. The K-B placements: do you want them explicit and shared with AJ and Noah, as the course's workbook implies, or private? The course says cross-check with your boss. Is Chris that boss for this, given the review-authority question is still open?

content.text:
Fable 5.1 read all 31 lessons and 26 PDFs, then wrote the summary, the department plan, and your recommendations. They're in a new private repo, pushed to GitHub and added to the DEV area index (`PROGRAM.md`).

**Repo:** `DEV/RunningTheRoom`, https://github.com/erash11/RunningTheRoom. On the Mac, get it with `gh repo clone erash11/RunningTheRoom`. The course videos and PDFs stay on Drive and are never committed.

## What this is
"Running The Room" is a paid Old Bull Performance course by Dr Jason Weber, a former AFL high-performance manager. Its argument: departments buy technology faster than they build the people, shared language and procedures that turn it into decisions, and the fix is writing that discipline down. It has four modules:
1. **People and language before technology.** A grid that rates staff on knowledge and behaviour, and an audit of your tech stack.
2. **Technology into defensible decisions.** Mapping each tool to a question and an owner, monitoring vs testing, decision gates set in advance, and the reliability math for telling real change from noise.
3. **Discipline equals freedom.** Every meeting is named as one of four types (Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build). A running decision log, red/amber/green readouts, and meetings used as practice reps for junior staff.
4. **The integration problem.** Five points where good technical work fails to reach a decision, and a way to structure the handover between Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance.

## The plan (`docs/01_department_plan.md`)
Four phases, in the same order as the modules. Each phase has its steps, what it produces, an owner, and a way to tell whether staff are actually using it. There is also a section on what has to be installed so the department runs without the leader.

## Recommendations (`docs/02_recommendations.md`)
The main challenge: your summer scorecard proves the course's point. Work that depended on you writing a document averaged 0.23, and the only two items that scored 1.0 were practices other people adopted. Stop counting documents; count adoption.
- **Education:** cut the education goal to two pieces at the Oct 15 checkpoint unless one shows real use. Move the teaching into meetings you already run.
- **Staff meeting:** make the announced biweekly Applied Performance staff meeting actually happen, with named segments and a decision log in Teams.
- **Kitman vs MyLink:** treat it as a two-option decision to make with Chris by Oct 15. First ask what either platform answers that your current stack can't. If nothing, the answer may be neither.
- **Staff:**
  - AJ is framed as your likely successor.
  - Noah gets a four-step ladder of practice reps.
  - Linda is deliberately not rated, because the sources say nothing about her knowledge or behaviour.
- **Projects:** every project gets a call to continue, reshape, pause or stop. For example, the Research repository MVP and Transformative Athlete Experience stop, and the HPI protocol shrinks to one sport's column of the capability matrix.

**First week (about 85 minutes, done by Oct 1):**
1. Do your own knowledge-and-behaviour self-audit and file it in your PD folder, which is due Sept 30 anyway.
2. Rewrite the next staff meeting invite and your next 1:1 invite with AJ so each states the meeting type, goal, length and prep. Set up the Teams decision-log channel.
3. Send Kenny the overdue email agreeing the plan for the tech inventory.

**Open questions only you can answer:**
- Is AJ the successor, and will you tell him and Chris before December?
- Which ground is yours under the new Athlete Health structure?
- Will you really cut the education goal on Oct 15?
- What gap would Kitman or MyLink actually fill?
- Should the staff ratings be shared with AJ and Noah or kept private?

**Things to know:**
- The synthesis agent pulled the July 29 all-staff meeting transcript from Fireflies to account for the new structure: Carrie's promotion, sport care teams, and software approval now going through general counsel.
- The transcripts are unchecked speech-to-text drafts. The PDFs are the authority, and the docs cite them by page.
- Status report #3 (due 9/25) is still owed.

I can turn the plan and recommendations into a private web page if you'd find that easier to read or share.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\memory-write

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index. `name:` follows the rule below.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## The `name:` field — bare kebab slug

**`name:` = the filename stem minus its leading type token, kebab-cased.** The type
already lives in `metadata.type` and the filename already carries the prefix; repeating
it in `name:` is the third copy.

| File | `name:` |
|---|---|
| `project_automation-cadence.md` | `automation-cadence` |
| `user_sports-teams.md` | `sports-teams` |
| `reference_baylor-house-style.md` | `baylor-house-style` |
| `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` | `project-idea-capture` |

Note the last row: strip only the **leading** token. `feedback_project_idea_capture.md`
is a feedback memory *about* project-idea capture — its name keeps the word `project`.

`[[links]]` target this bare name, never the filename and never a prefixed variant.

This rule exists because it was previously unwritten: an audit on 2026-09-02 found the
corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, which broke 37 links. Both forms look right in
isolation, so without a stated rule the split regrows on every write.

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the Windows-machine slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Write only to the current machine's slug.** Both machines are active as of 2026-09-10: Mac slugs are `-Users-kristinarash-*`, Windows slugs are `C--Users-eric-rash-*`. A fact written to the other machine's slug is never auto-injected here (memsearch still finds it). Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

## Verification Gate

After every write:

1. Read the exact destination back and require the intended fact to appear once in the intended tier.
2. Re-run the Tier B character cap check after the write.
3. Check the surrounding section for an unresolved contradiction or stale duplicate. Resolve it or report `FAIL`.
4. For Tier A, verify the new file has valid frontmatter and the memory index pointer resolves to it.
5. Distinguish persisted state from activation: the write can pass now, but next-session injection remains unverified until a later session observes it.

Report `PASS` only when persistence, uniqueness, tier placement, caps, and pointers are verified. Report `FAIL` with the target path and failed check otherwise. Do not emit “Saved” before read-back succeeds.

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.
